newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: BSE experts to study possible blood transmission.
newsitem.headline: BSE experts to study possible blood transmission.

text.p: Medical experts meet next month to examine the possible risk of transmitting Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease through medicinal products containing animal tissues or human blood, the World Health Organisation said on Tuesday.
The WHO meeting in Geneva, scheduled for March 24-26, will bring together 40 to 50 international medical experts on animal or human transmissible spongiform encephalopathies.

The United Nations health agency is coordinating worldwide surveillance amid fears that mad cow disease or Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE) can cross over to humans in a new form of the brain-wasting Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease.
The experts will examine the epidemiology of both classical, Creutzfeldt-Jakob neurological disease and a new variant, of which 16 cases have been confirmed in Britain and France.
Their recommendations, also expected to cover potential maternal transmission and safety of gelatin, will be issued to the 191 member states of the United Nations agency.

Experts will review the risk of possible transmission, via medicinal products containing bovine and possibly ovine tissues, of animal transmissible spongiform encephalopathies as well as the possible transmission of human transmissible spongiform encephalopathies via medicinal products containing human tissues including blood and blood products, according to Dr. Francois-Xavier Meslin.

"It doesn't mean there is any proof it can be transmitted via blood," Meslin told Reuters. "But this hypothesis has been made and we will look at the results of a study carried out very recently and see whether there is a real risk and how to mitigate it if that risk exists."
The experts will review results of a study made at the U.S. National Institute of Health in Bethesda, Maryland, according to the WHO expert.
Potential infectability through medicinal instruments including heart valves using animal collagen will also be examined, Meslin added.
